νομίζειν εἶναι τῶν διαθηκῶν τῆς ἐπαγγελίας. ζητήσεις δὲ μήποτε διὰ τοῦτο εἴρηται

γράφεται ἡ ἐπιστολή. [ii 13] νυνὶ δὲ ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ ὑμεῖς οἵ ποτε ὄντες μακρὰν
ἐγενήθητε ἐγγὺς ἐν τῷ αἵματι τοῦ Χριστοῦ. τὸ μακρὰν καὶ τὸ ἐγγὺς ὠνομάσθη ἀπὸ
τῶν τοπικῶς μακρὰν ἢ ἐγγύς, εἰς παράστασιν τῆς πόρρω τοῦ Θεοῦ προαιρέσεως καὶ
τῆς ἐγγιζούσης τῷ θελήματι αὐτοῦ· γινόμεθα δὲ ἐγγὺς καθαρθέντες τῷ αἵματι τοῦ
Χριστοῦ καὶ ταύτης τῆς τιμῆ ἀγορα θέντε . [ii 14a] αὐτὸς γάρ ἐστιν ἡ εἰρήνη ἡμῶν.
τηρητέον ὅτι, ὥσπερ ἐστὶ λόγο ὁ Χριστὸς καὶ οφία καὶ δύναμι καὶ ζωή, οὕτως καὶ
εἰρήνη· καὶ συνακτέον γε πάντα ἀπὸ πάσης γραφῆς ἃ ὀνομάζεται, ἵνα αὐτὸν
ἀκριβέστερον νοήσωμεν. ὥσπερ οὖν ὁ ἔχων αὐτὸν ἔχει λόγον, ὅτε αὐτὸν ζητή α
εὗρεν ὡς λόγον (τὸ δὲ ἀνάλογον καὶ ἐπὶ οφία καὶ δικαιο ύνη ἔχει), οὕτως
ζητήσωμεν αὐτὸν καὶ ὡς εἰρήνην, ἵνα αὐτὸν ἔχωμεν καθώς ἐστιν Εἰρήνη καὶ εἰρήνη
πάντων τῶν λογικῶν· ὁ δὲ μὴ ἔχων τὴν εἰρήνην οὐκ ἔχει τὸν Χριστόν. 12 Eph. ii.
14b, 15, 17 [ὁ ποιήσας τὰ ἀμφότερα ἓν καὶ τὸ μεσότοιχον τοῦ φραγμοῦ λύσας, τὴν
ἔχθραν ἐν τῇ σαρκὶ αὐτοῦ, τὸν νόμον τῶν ἐντολῶν ἐν δόγμασιν καταλύσας, ἵνα τοὺς
δύο κτίσῃ εἰς ἕνα καινὸν ἄνθρωπον ... καὶ ἐλθὼν εὐηγγελίσατο εἰρήνην ὑμῖν τοῖς
μακρὰν καὶ εἰρήνην τοῖς ἐγγύς.] [Ὠριγένης δέ φησι] ταῦτα λέγεσθαι περὶ τῶν
θειοτέρων δυνάμεων καὶ τῶν ἀπὸ ἀνθρώπων σωζομένων, τῶν μὲν θειοτέρων
δυνάμεων οὐσῶν καὶ πρότερον ἐγγὺς τῶν δὲ ἀνθρώπων μακράν (ἐφαρμόσει δὲ
τούτοις ὁ ταῦτα λέγων τὸ εἰρηνο ποιή α διὰ τοῦ αἵματο τοῦ ταυροῦ αὐτοῦ εἴτε τὰ
ἐπὶ τῆ γῆ εἴτε τὰ ἐν τοῖ οὐρανοῖ , καὶ ὅλα τὰ κατὰ τὸν τόπον οὕτω διηγήσεται), τῶν
μὲν κρειττό νων δυνάμεων ὅτι ἐν φιλίᾳ ἦν πρὸς τὸν θεόν, τῶν δὲ ἐν κόσμῳ
ἀνθρώπων ὅτι ἐν ἔχθρᾳ ἦν πρὸς αὐτόν· καὶ αὕτη ἡ ἔχθρα τὸ μεσότοιχον ἦν τοῦ
φραγμοῦ κωλῦον τοῦ ἑνοῦσθαι τὴν ἀνθρώπων φύσιν τῇ μακαριότητι τῶν
κρειττόνων. τοῦτο οὖν τὸ μεσότοιχον τοῦ φραγμοῦ, ἔχθρα τυγχάνον, ἐλύθη διὰ τοῦ
ἐνην θρωπηκέναι τὸν σωτῆρα ἡμῶν, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο λέγεται λελύσθαι ἐν τῇ σαρκὶ
pass_a_gloss: The open tip cut mid phrase; rem early continues with the wills of the thoughts. On the line we were by nature children of wrath even as the rest, those who introduce spiritual natures from the beginning have no easy reply. How can one who is by nature a son of God also be said to be by nature a son of wrath. We think that through the body of humiliation we became children of wrath by nature when our understanding clung to evils from youth, for according to Solomon there is no one on the earth who does good and does not sin. On Ephesians 2:6, he raised us and seated us with him in the heavenly places, the simpler reader takes the past tense by Gods foreknowledge and predestination speaking the future as already done. The reader who contemplates Christs kingdom as intelligible will say the person already holy is not in flesh in the deeper sense even if simpler people say he is in flesh, and is not on earth even if the senses see him on earth, for one who is in spirit is not on earth, and none of those in the heavenly places is in flesh but already in spirit. Such dispositions and the grasp of things so great are not earthly but heavenly. All who already have their citizenship in heaven sit with Christ in the heavenly places if indeed the kingdom of God is within us, so that we have sat with Christ and are settled with the Wisdom and the Word of God. On Ephesians 2:12, that you were then without Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, strangers to the covenants of promise, without hope and without God in the world, Origen answers those who invent a new polity with nothing in common with Israel. The past tense you were then implies that now they are no longer without Christ or alienated. All who understand the spiritual law and live by it are made kin to Israels polity more than the bodily Jews. The one without Christ and alienated from Israels polity is also reckoned a stranger to the covenants of promise. Ask whether they are called without God in this world because in Gods foreknowledge the addressees were not without God. On Ephesians 2:13, far and near are borrowed from spatial distance to show a purpose far from God versus one drawing near to his will. We become near when cleansed by the blood of Christ and bought with that price. On Ephesians 2:14a, he himself is our peace. Just as Christ is Word and Wisdom and Power and Life, so also Peace. Gather from all Scripture the names given him. Having him as Peace is having Christ; without the peace one does not have Christ. On Ephesians 2:14 through 17, both made one, the dividing wall of the fence which is enmity broken in his flesh, the law of commandments abolished in decrees so as to create one new man, peace preached to the far and the near. Origen reads this of the more divine powers already near and of humans saved who were far. The better powers were in friendship with God; humans in the world were in enmity. That enmity was the wall blocking union with the blessedness of the better. The wall that is enmity was dissolved by our Saviors becoming human, and so is said to have been broken in his flesh.
pass_b_english: As for “we were by nature children of wrath, even as the rest,” we do not know what those who introduce spiritual natures from the beginning will say. How can one who is by nature a son of God be said to be by nature a son of wrath? Let them answer. We think that through the body of humiliation we became children of wrath by nature when our understanding clung to evils from youth; for according to Solomon there is no one righteous on the earth who does good and does not sin.

Eph. 2:6: “and raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places.” Origen says: the one who takes “he raised and seated” more simply will say it is spoken according to God’s foreknowledge and predestination, as what will be already spoken of as done. But the one who contemplates Christ’s kingdom as intelligible will not hesitate to say that the person already holy, just as he is not “in flesh” even if simpler people say he is in flesh, so he is not “on earth” even if to the senses he is seen on earth. For the one in spirit is not on earth, and none of those in the heavenly places is in flesh but already in spirit.

Such dispositions, and the grasp of things so great and of such a kind, are not earthly but heavenly; all who already have their citizenship in heaven sit with Christ in the heavenly places, if indeed the kingdom of God is within us—so that in this way we have sat in the heavenly places, seated with Christ and settled with the Wisdom and the Word of God.

Eph. 2:12: “that you were at that time without Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world.” Origen says: against those who think that believers in Christ do not live Israel’s polity but some other new one with nothing in common with that, there is a fine observation here. “For you were,” he says, “at that time without Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel”—as if now they are no longer without Christ, nor alienated from Israel’s polity. For all who understand the spiritual law and live by it are made kin to Israel’s polity, and more so than the bodily Jews. It follows that the one without Christ and alienated from Israel’s polity is also reckoned a stranger to the covenants of promise.
You will ask whether for this reason they are called “without God in this world”: because, as far as God’s foreknowledge goes, those to whom the letter is written were not without God.

Eph. 2:13: “But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have become near by the blood of Christ.” “Far” and “near” are named from things spatially far or near, to show a purpose far from God and one drawing near to his will. We become near when cleansed by the blood of Christ and bought with that price.

Eph. 2:14a: “For he himself is our peace.” Mark that, just as Christ is Word and Wisdom and Power and Life, so also Peace; and one must gather from all Scripture the names he is given, that we may understand him more exactly. So as the one who has him has Word when he has sought him and found him as Word (and likewise for Wisdom and righteousness), let us also seek him as Peace, that we may have him as he is Peace, and peace of all rational beings. The one who does not have the peace does not have Christ.

Eph. 2:14b–15, 17: “who made both one and broke down the dividing wall of the fence, the enmity in his flesh, abolishing the law of the commandments in decrees, that he might create the two into one new man … and coming he preached peace to you who were far and peace to those near.” Origen says: these things are said of the more divine powers and of those saved from among humans—the more divine powers being near even before, humans far (and to these the speaker will fit “having made peace through the blood of his cross, whether things on earth or things in the heavens,” and will narrate the whole passage so). The better powers were in friendship with God; humans in the world were in enmity toward him; and that enmity was the dividing wall of the fence, hindering human nature from being united to the blessedness of the better. So this dividing wall of the fence, being enmity, was broken through our Savior’s becoming human, and for that reason it is said to have been broken in his flesh.
